# Value Chain Position — HAIER

## 1. Stages Occupied

| Value Chain Stage | Company Role (1 sentence) | Bargaining Power vs Upstream | Bargaining Power vs Downstream | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Input buyer (raw materials / components) | Haier does not supply raw materials — it buys steel, aluminium, copper and plastics/foam from third-party mills, metal traders and component makers, and hedges the resulting commodity exposure with futures and supplier volume-price agreements | **Mid** | n/a (this row is upstream-only) | Top 5 suppliers combined = RMB34,914.80m of purchases, 16.4% of FY2025 total procurement, of which RMB10,534.53m (5.0% of purchases) was to Haier-group-affiliated related parties; company explicitly certifies no single supplier exceeded 50% of purchases and there is no "severe dependence on a small number of suppliers" [FY2025 Annual Report (SSE, China ASBE), Section 3(7)A/B, p.43-44]. Company runs a dedicated commodity-hedging policy ("大宗原材料套期保值业务管理办法") and uses supplier "volume-price betting" (量价对赌) to blunt swings [FY2025 Annual Report (SSE, China ASBE), p.58, item 3] |
| Manufacturer / processor | Core role — designs, engineers and assembles refrigerators, washers, air conditioners, water heaters and kitchen appliances at owned plants across 30+ countries (60+ overseas factories) under the Haier, Casarte, Leader, GE Appliances, Candy, Fisher & Paykel and AQUA brands | **Mid** (see input-buyer row above; the constraint is the global commodity price level, not any single supplier's leverage) | **Weak-Mid** | Raw materials were 84.0% of the household-appliance segment's cost of sales in FY2025, up from 82.0% in FY2024 [FY2025 Annual Report (SSE, China ASBE), p.23 cost-structure table] — the company absorbs, rather than fully passes through, input-cost rises (see §2) |
| Distributor / channel (China + overseas retail and third-party-brand distribution) | Sells mainly through third-party retail chains, appliance specialists and online marketplaces (JD.com, Tmall) in China, and through named/unnamed local retailers overseas; also runs a smaller "Other businesses" segment (RMB39,211m FY2025) that includes channel distribution of third-party brands and logistics services, plus a standalone trading business (RMB3,859.8m FY2025 revenue, down 6.93% YoY) | n/a (see Manufacturer row) | **Weak-Mid** | No single customer or distributor reached 20% of revenue (top 5 combined = 19.6% of FY2025 sales, certified as not severely dependent) [FY2025 Annual Report (SSE, China ASBE), Section 3(7)A/B, p.43-44], but the filing itself states distributors, retailers and online platforms "may place orders with us at such time and in such quantities as they deem appropriate" — no minimum-volume or contract-term commitment disclosed for any channel [FY2025 Annual Report (HKEX, IFRS), "Relationship with Customers," p.80] |
| End-customer-facing brand (owned e-commerce / brand stores + multi-tier brand portfolio) | Sells directly to households via the Haier Smart Home App, brand flagship stores and premium sub-brand Casarte, alongside mass-market Haier and value-tier Leader, aiming to earn a brand premium rather than compete purely on price | n/a | **Weak-Mid** | Premiumization is real at the product-mix level — Casarte's Refinement/Radiance series reached 43% of Casarte retail sales in Q1 2026, up 13 points [Q1 2026 Report (HKEX), p.3] — but FY2025 group gross margin still fell 1.1 percentage points to 26.7%, because "Q4 domestic-market rises in copper and other bulk materials, plus intensifying domestic competition, accelerated the industry-wide decline in average selling price" [FY2025 Annual Report (SSE, China ASBE), MD&A, p.22] — i.e., premium mix gains were not enough to lift blended price against a price war |

Bargaining power bands:
- **Strong:** Company sets price, dictates terms, has alternatives
- **Mid:** Negotiated outcomes, no extreme leverage either way
- **Weak:** Price-taker, terms imposed, few alternatives

## 2. Input Cost Pass-Through

Haier does not pass input-cost increases through to customers on any disclosed lag or contractual formula — no escalator, indexed-pricing or cost-plus clause appears anywhere in the pool. Instead it manages commodity risk financially, through hedging (a dedicated internal policy governing bulk-commodity futures hedging) and negotiated "volume-price betting" arrangements with suppliers, and operationally, through a cost-reduction program ("极致成本战略," global co-ordinated procurement, material-code standardization) [FY2025 Annual Report (SSE, China ASBE), p.22, p.58 item 3]. The evidence that this financial/operational buffer is incomplete is direct: FY2025 group gross margin fell 1.1 percentage points to 26.7% because Q4 copper and other bulk-material price rises, combined with intensifying domestic competition, drove the industry average selling price down faster than the company's cost cuts could offset [FY2025 Annual Report (SSE, China ASBE), MD&A, p.22]. The same pattern repeated in Q1 2026: group gross margin was 25.3%, down 0.1 percentage points year-on-year, as "the positive impact from global supply-chain layout and extreme cost optimization was offset by high tariffs and rising bulk material prices" in overseas markets [Q1 2026 Report (HKEX), p.4]. In China specifically, hedging and cost programs did lift margin year-on-year in Q1 2026 [Q1 2026 Report (HKEX), p.4] — so the mitigation tools work at the margin, but they are cost-absorption tools, not price pass-through to the end customer.

**Supplier / input concentration (quantify).** Top 5 suppliers combined took RMB34,914.80m of FY2025 purchases, 16.4% of the year's total procurement spend; of that, RMB10,534.53m (5.0% of total purchases) went to related parties inside the Haier Group [FY2025 Annual Report (SSE, China ASBE), Section 3(7)A, p.43]. The company explicitly checked "not applicable" to both "purchases from a single supplier exceed 50% of the total" and "severe dependence on a small number of suppliers" [FY2025 Annual Report (SSE, China ASBE), Section 3(7)B, p.44]. No single-source or sole-source input or component is separately named in the pool. The real dependency is not on any one vendor but on a concentrated set of global commodity inputs — steel, aluminium, copper, and plastics/foam are named as the specific raw materials whose price volatility is a disclosed principal risk, and together raw materials are 84.0% of the appliance segment's cost of sales (up from 82.0% in FY2024) [FY2025 Annual Report (SSE, China ASBE), p.23, p.58 item 3]. This is a market-wide commodity-price exposure, not a bargaining-power problem with a specific supplier — the filing does not quantify a commodity-price sensitivity (e.g., "a 10% copper move changes gross margin by X bps"), so the size of that exposure beyond the 84%-of-COGS weight is not proven from available data.

## 3. Customer Pricing Power

Haier cannot reliably raise prices without losing volume in its largest market. The company's own FY2025 MD&A attributes the year's 1.1-point gross-margin decline directly to an accelerating industry-wide fall in average selling price in China, driven by hyper-competitive conditions on top of rising input costs — the opposite of pricing power [FY2025 Annual Report (SSE, China ASBE), MD&A, p.22]. The one lever that has worked is mix, not price: Casarte's premium Refinement/Radiance product lines grew from 30% to 43% of Casarte's own retail sales in a single year (Q1 2025 to Q1 2026), and the mass-market Haier-brand "bundle" package rose from 17% to 25% of Haier-brand retail sales over the same period [Q1 2026 Report (HKEX), p.3] — but this is premiumization within the portfolio, not evidence the company can raise list prices on a given product without volume loss. Overseas, the North America segment cites "dynamic pricing" as one of several efficiency levers used to offset tariff and demand pressure [Q1 2026 Report (HKEX), p.4], but no explicit price increase, its date, or its volume effect is disclosed anywhere in the pool — this claim is Not proven from available data beyond the general "dynamic pricing" language. Tariffs on China-linked appliance exports to the US are explicitly said to have "weighed on the Company's performance in the North American market" [Q1 2026 Report (HKEX), p.2] rather than being shown as fully recovered through higher US shelf prices.

## 4. Economic Control Verdict

**Mixed.** Upstream, Haier has real (if not dominant) leverage: no single supplier or supplier group is concentrated, it hedges commodity exposure with a dedicated futures policy, and it negotiates volume-price terms with suppliers — none of which stopped Q4-2025 copper and bulk-material inflation from compressing margin, but the supplier relationship itself is not the constraint (§2). Downstream, the company is structurally weaker: its own filings show it could not raise blended prices fast enough to offset input-cost and tariff inflation in FY2025 and Q1 2026, because both its China retail/distribution channel and its overseas retail channel order "at such time and in such quantities as they deem appropriate" with no binding volume commitment [FY2025 Annual Report (HKEX, IFRS), "Relationship with Customers," p.80], and China's appliance market is explicitly described as intensely price-competitive.

## 5. The Single Biggest Bargaining Risk

The China domestic retail/distribution channel — supplying roughly half of group revenue on discretionary, non-contracted order terms inside an industry-wide price war that already erased Haier's cost-reduction gains and cut FY2025 gross margin by 1.1 points [FY2025 Annual Report (SSE, China ASBE), MD&A, p.22; "Relationship with Customers," p.80] — is the relationship most likely to hurt the company further if it deteriorates.

## business-model / 07_business-quality.md

_Source: `business-model/07_business-quality.md`_

# Business Quality — HAIER

Upstream inputs read: `02_business-identity.md`, `03_segment-map.md`, `05_customer-geography.md`, `10_external-dependency.md`, `11_capital-allocation-governance.md` — all present. No upstream gap to flag.

**Sector overlay (step 2b):** `02_business-identity.md` §3a already checked Haier against `frameworks/SECTOR_OVERLAYS.md` and found no matching row — the company is not SaaS, a bank/insurer/REIT, a commodity/oil & gas producer, a store-based retailer (Haier does not run its own store network as the primary channel), a telecom, an asset manager, or pharma. **No sector overlay for multi-brand global home-appliance manufacturer — generic 11-factor scoring applies.** The "generic operating company" factor set (volume, price/mix, capital intensity, cyclicality, disclosure) is used below, consistent with the identity agent's classification.

## 1. Quality Factor Table

| Quality Factor | Score /100 | Evidence | Comment |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Pricing power *(higher = better)* | 38 | Gross margin fell from 30.9% (FY2021) to 26.3% (FY2025), a 460bp decline over five years [Haier Smart Home Co Ltd SHSE 600690 Financials.xls, tab: Ratios, Gross Margin % FY2021–FY2025]. Company MD&A attributes part of the FY2025 decline to Q4 copper/bulk-material price rises overwhelming its cost-reduction program [FY2025 Annual Report (China ASBE, SSE 600690), MD&A margin discussion, p.22]. The segment map flags explicit "price-war risk in a fragmented, oversupplied sub-industry" for Air Solutions [`03_segment-map.md`, §1]. | Premium-brand mix (Casarte) and China category leadership (47.7% refrigerator share, 47.4% washer share, offline) give some ASP support, but the company cannot reliably push through input-cost inflation — gross margin is the purer read of pricing power and it is trending down, not up. |
| Repeat / recurring revenue *(higher = better)* | 32 | Core products (refrigerators, washers, ACs, water heaters) are durable goods bought once every several years, not a subscription or consumable-refill model. No recurring-revenue metric (service contracts, consumables, subscription) is disclosed as a distinct line anywhere in the pool; the closest quasi-recurring item is the undifferentiated "Other Business" bucket (channel distribution, logistics, small appliances — 13.0% of FY2025 revenue) which is not broken out further [`03_segment-map.md`, §1 and §3]. | This is a repeat-purchase business on an 8–15-year replacement cycle (inference, not from filings, on typical appliance life — not itself disclosed), not a recurring-revenue business. |
| Customer stickiness *(higher = better)* | 32 | No long-term contract or minimum-volume commitment is disclosed with any channel: distributors, retailers and online platforms "may place orders with us at such time and in such quantities as they deem appropriate" [FY2025 Annual Report (HKEX, IFRS), "Relationship with Customers", p.80, cited in `05_customer-geography.md` §1]. Top-5 customers combined are only 19.6% of FY2025 sales, and the company certifies no severe dependence on any small customer group [FY2025 Annual Report (SSE, China ASBE), Section 3(7)A/B, pp.43-44]. | Diversified channel base is a de-risking feature, not a stickiness feature — there is no contractual lock-in anywhere in the chain, and end-consumer repurchase is a fresh competitive decision each cycle, not an automatic renewal. |
| Margin stability *(higher = better)* | 52 | Gross margin swung from 30.9% (FY21/FY22) down to 26.3–27.5% (FY23–FY25) — a real, multi-year step-down, not noise [Financials.xls, tab: Ratios]. But EBITDA margin actually rose over the same window, from 8.0% (FY21) to a peak 9.8% (FY24) before pulling back to 8.8% (FY25), and net income margin rose from 5.8% (FY21) to 6.5% (FY24/FY25) [same source] — SG&A margin fell from 20.7% (FY21) to 15.8% (FY25), offsetting the gross-margin erosion. | Mixed: the line that measures pure pricing/cost power (gross margin) is trending down and sits at a five-year low; the line that measures bottom-line outcome (net margin) is near a five-year high, propped up by SG&A leverage and by the now-fading China trade-in subsidy pulling volume forward through FY24. See §4 for the reconciliation. |
| Capital intensity *(low intensity = high score)* | 45 | Capex ran CNY8,851.6m in FY2025 (2.9% of RMB302,347m revenue), down from CNY10,541.6m (3.8% of revenue) in FY2023 [Financials.xls, tab: Cash Flow, Capital Expenditure row; Financials.xls, tab: Income Statement, Total Revenue row]. Capex still runs ~1.19x FY2025 D&A (CNY7,457.1m) — some growth spend, not pure maintenance [`11_capital-allocation-governance.md`, capex row]. Segment assets/revenue run 0.54x–1.11x, with Air Solutions assets nearly doubling FY24→FY25 (RMB32,729m → RMB57,700m, +76%) against only 9.6% revenue growth on acquisition-driven asset additions [`03_segment-map.md`, §1]. | A global manufacturing footprint (30+ countries) with meaningful, if moderating, capex — not asset-light, but not as capital-heavy as heavy industry either. |
| Competitive intensity *(low intensity = high score)* | 24 | The CapIQ competitor list names a crowded global field: Midea (RMB68.2bn LTM revenue), LG Electronics (RMB63.8bn), Panasonic (RMB51.3bn), Gree (RMB25.5bn), Whirlpool, Electrolux, BSH/Bosch, Hisense, Arçelik, plus dozens of regional players (Blue Star, Amber, Dixon, Voltas-adjacent names in India; Godrej & Boyce) [Haier Smart Home Co Ltd SHSE 600690 Competitors.rtf]. The segment map independently flags "price-war risk in a fragmented, oversupplied sub-industry" for the Air Solutions segment, and notes China's central-air-conditioning market fell 7.4% in FY2025 [`03_segment-map.md`, §1]. | This is one of the most crowded consumer-durables categories globally, with multiple scale competitors in every product line and every major geography Haier sells into — a structurally high-rivalry industry regardless of any one company's share position (share position is the moat agent's question, not this row's). |
| Industry rate-of-change / disruption risk *(low rate-of-change = high score)* | 72 | The core categories (refrigerators, washing machines, air conditioners, water heaters) are mature technologies with decades-long stable competitive rosters — the same handful of global brands (Haier, Whirlpool, Electrolux, LG, Samsung, Midea, Bosch, Panasonic) have led the category for 20+ years, per the competitor list itself [Haier Smart Home Co Ltd SHSE 600690 Competitors.rtf]. No AI/platform-style discontinuity is disclosed anywhere in the pool; "smart home" features are incremental, not category-redefining, in the filings' own MD&A language. | This is closer to the "paints, sanitaryware, fans" stable-winners example than to EV/biotech/quick-commerce — the rules of the game (brand, distribution scale, manufacturing cost, working capital) have not changed materially in decades. See §4: this factor scoring above 40 means the §24 Filter-5 fast-changing-industry flag does NOT trip here. |
| Regulatory dependence *(low dependence = high score)* | 34 | External-dependency scores "Government policy" as **High**: China's national appliance trade-in subsidy (15% of sale price, capped at RMB1,500/unit) is a named direct demand driver, and the company's own 2026 outlook warns of "high base pressure" as the subsidy effect fades [`10_external-dependency.md`, §1, Government policy row]. US/EU tariffs are a second, separately-named regulatory/trade-policy drag on the North America segment [same source, Geopolitics row]. EU F-Gas and energy-efficiency rules are a partial offsetting tailwind for the commercial-refrigeration line, but are not large enough to flip the overall read. | Two of the four "High" external variables the dependency agent identified are government-policy-driven (subsidy, tariffs) — this is a real, not theoretical, dependence, and it has already moved reported volume and margin in FY2025. |
| Commodity dependence *(low dependence = high score)* | 18 | Raw materials (steel, aluminium, copper, plastics/foam) are 84.0% of the household-appliance segment's cost of sales in FY2025, up from 82.0% in FY2024 [FY2025 Annual Report (China ASBE, SSE 600690), cost-structure table, p.23]. Named as a top-ten principal risk by the company itself [same source, p.58, item 3]. No formal commodity sensitivity table is disclosed, but the FY2025 gross-margin decline is explicitly attributed in part to Q4 copper price rises overwhelming the cost-reduction program [same source, MD&A, p.22]. | At 84% of COGS, this is about as commodity-exposed as a manufacturer gets short of being a pure processor — active hedging (forwards, commodity futures under an internal policy) mitigates but does not eliminate the exposure [`10_external-dependency.md`, §3]. |
| Cyclicality *(low cyclicality = high score)* | 34 | The company's own #1 disclosed principal risk is macro/consumer-cycle demand risk, explicitly tied to the Chinese property-market slowdown and to "high US interest rates plus tariff-driven inflation curbing US appliance consumption" [FY2025 Annual Report (China ASBE, SSE 600690), p.58 item 1; p.3]. China's central air-conditioning market fell 7.4% in FY2025 on the same real-estate linkage [`03_segment-map.md`, §1, Air Solutions row]. The now-fading government subsidy adds a second layer of demand volatility (pull-forward, then air-pocket) on top of the underlying replacement/new-household cycle. | Household appliances are durable-good, income- and housing-cycle-sensitive purchases — this is not a business with demand insulated from the macro or property cycle in its two largest markets (China, US). |
| Disclosure quality *(higher = better)* | 68 | Dual-filer with two audited, unqualified-opinion annual reports for the same FY2025 period (China ASBE/SSE and IFRS/HKEX), reconciling to within 0.006% at the revenue line [`03_segment-map.md`, intro]. Segment note discloses profit, assets AND liabilities by segment (not revenue-only) [`03_segment-map.md`, §3]. FX/rate sensitivity tables and related-party-transaction disclosure are both present and quantified [`10_external-dependency.md`, §2; `11_capital-allocation-governance.md`, related-party row]. Offsetting gaps: the "Other Business" catch-all is 13.0% of revenue (above the 10% materiality threshold) with no further product-level split; no unit-volume, capacity-utilization, or segment-by-geography profit matrix is disclosed anywhere in the pool [`03_segment-map.md`, §3]; no post-2019 earnings transcript or investor deck exists in the data pool [`00_data-triage.md`, §3]. | A genuinely well-documented dual-standard filer (better than most single-listed peers on segment granularity), held back from a higher score by the large undisclosed catch-all bucket and the complete absence of unit/volume and capacity data that would let a reader separate price from volume. |

Bands used: 0–20 Very weak, 21–40 Weak, 41–60 Mixed/Average, 61–80 Strong, 81–100 Very strong.

## 2. Aggregate Quality Score

**42/100 (Weak, upper end).**

Row scores, sorted low to high: Commodity dependence 18, Competitive intensity 24, Repeat/recurring revenue 32, Customer stickiness 32, Regulatory dependence 34, Cyclicality 34, Pricing power 38, Capital intensity 45, Margin stability 52, Disclosure quality 68, Industry rate-of-change 72. **Band anchor check:** the second-lowest row is Competitive intensity at 24; the aggregate (42) sits 18 points above it, inside the ~20-point ceiling the anchor rule allows. Weighting: heaviest weight goes to the five structural-quality rows that cluster in the Weak band — commodity dependence, competitive intensity, cyclicality, regulatory dependence, and pricing power — because these describe the underlying economics of selling a commodity-input, price-competed durable good into a cyclical, policy-sensitive demand base; these carry roughly 55% of the judgment weight. Margin stability and capital intensity (both Mixed/Average, ~30% weight combined) reflect that the company still converts a difficult cost/competitive backdrop into stable-to-improving bottom-line margins through SG&A discipline. Disclosure quality and the rate-of-change row (~15% weight) are real positives — the industry is not fast-changing and the company discloses more than most peers — but neither offsets a business built on a thin, commodity-exposed, cyclically-exposed core.

## 3. Strongest Factor & Weakest Factor

| | Factor | Score | Why |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Strongest | Industry rate-of-change / disruption risk | 72 | Home appliances are a mature, slow-changing category; the same handful of global brands have led every major product line for 20+ years, with no platform-style discontinuity visible in the filings. |
| Weakest | Commodity dependence | 18 | Raw materials are 84.0% of the appliance segment's cost of sales, a company-named principal risk, and the demonstrated cause of the FY2025 gross-margin decline via Q4 copper price rises. |

## 4. Read

This is a conservatively financed, cyclical global manufacturer of a commodity-input, price-competed durable good — not a durable compounder and not a fast-changing technology bet either. The industry rate-of-change row scored 72 (above the 40 threshold), so the §24 Filter-5 "sector / technology-cycle bet" flag does **not** apply here; the risk in this name is old-economy cyclicality and cost-pass-through, not disruption. The single quality factor a buyer should watch over the next 24 months is **gross margin**: it fell from 30.9% (FY2021) to 26.3% (FY2025) even as net income margin held near a five-year high (6.5%, FY2024/FY2025) — the gap was closed by SG&A leverage (20.7%→15.8% of revenue) and by a China trade-in subsidy that management's own FY2026 outlook says is now past its "high base," with growth "expected to face pressure" [FY2025 Annual Report (China ASBE, SSE 600690), p.3, p.20-21]. Reconciling the two readings: net margin and EBITDA margin (FY24 peak 9.8%) look near-cycle-peak because they were flattered by SG&A cuts and subsidy-driven volume, while gross margin — the cleaner read on underlying pricing power versus commodity cost — is at a trough, not a peak. Return on capital tells the same story: it peaked at 9.1% in FY2024 and pulled back to 8.0% in FY2025 and 7.6% on an LTM basis (Mar-2026) [Financials.xls, tab: Ratios, Return on Capital %], consistent with a business coming off a subsidy-assisted high rather than one compounding returns structurally upward. A buyer should treat FY2024's margin and ROIC prints as the cyclical high-water mark, not the sustainable run-rate, and should expect further gross-margin and ROIC pressure if commodity costs stay elevated and the subsidy tailwind keeps fading as management itself now expects.

## business-model / 08_competitive-map.md

_Source: `business-model/08_competitive-map.md`_

# Competitive Map — HAIER

Both required upstream inputs are present: `business-model/02_business-identity.md` and `business-model/03_segment-map.md`.

## 1. Dominant Segment

Household Food Storage & Cooking Solutions — refrigerators/freezers plus kitchen appliances, reported as one segment with two product-line splits — is Haier Smart Home's dominant segment: 41.7% of FY2025 external revenue (RMB125,975m of RMB302,347m) and 43.4% of segment profit before tax [`03_segment-map.md`, citing FY2025 Annual Report (SSE, CAS), Note 11(1), pp.222–223]. Refrigerators/freezers alone are 27.9% of revenue and the larger of the two product lines.

## 2. Named Competitors

Selection basis: Haier's own Chinese-language annual report discusses market share and industry rank ("行业第二", "位居行业前二") without naming specific rival companies by name in the pool extract reviewed. The company-level "named by company" source is therefore thin. The names below come from the S&P Capital IQ competitor-relationship export in the data pool (`Haier Smart Home Co Ltd SHSE 600690 Competitors.rtf`), which is built from third-party filings that name Haier alongside these companies as home-appliance rivals — this counts as "named by third party" per the selection criteria, and is the deepest competitor evidence available in the pool. All three below make refrigerators and/or kitchen appliances (Haier's dominant segment), and all are within roughly 3x of Haier's scale.

### Competitor A — Midea Group Co., Ltd. (SZSE:000333)

- **Ticker / listing:** Shenzhen Stock Exchange, 000333
- **Where they compete:** Global — household and central air conditioners, refrigerators, washing machines, kitchen appliances, and small appliances under the Midea brand; direct product overlap with Haier's dominant refrigerator/kitchen-appliance segment as well as air conditioning and laundry [`Haier Smart Home Co Ltd SHSE 600690 Competitors.rtf`, business description sourced from Whirlpool Corporation (NYSE:WHR) 2026 Form 10-K, which names Midea as a home-appliance competitor alongside Haier].
- **Scale:** LTM total revenue $68,169.1m (as of LTM filing date 2026-04-29, USD, Capital IQ) vs. Haier's LTM total revenue $44,028.5m on the same comp-set basis — Midea is ~1.55x Haier's revenue [`Company Comparable Analysis Haier Smart Home Co Ltd .xls`, tab: Financial Data]. On Haier's own FY2025 audited revenue of RMB302,329m (≈$42bn), the ratio is similar.
- **Profitability / return on capital:** LTM gross margin 26.3%, LTM EBITDA margin 11.5%, LTM EBIT margin 9.8%, LTM net income margin 9.6% — versus Haier's own LTM EBIT margin of 6.9% and net margin of 6.3% on the identical comp-set basis [`Company Comparable Analysis Haier Smart Home Co Ltd .xls`, tab: Operating Statistics]. ROIC/ROE not disclosed in this comp export — margin is the only peer-economics figure available from the pool for Midea.
- **Source named in:** Capital IQ competitor export (third-party source document: Whirlpool Corporation 2026 Form 10-K); independently corroborated by inclusion in Haier's own Capital IQ comparable-company set (`Company Comparable Analysis Haier Smart Home Co Ltd .xls`), which groups Midea with Haier as a China appliance peer.
- **One-line read:** A larger, more diversified Chinese appliance conglomerate (adds robotics/building tech/industrial segments) that on this comp set earns a higher EBIT margin than Haier in the same product categories.

### Competitor B — Gree Electric Appliances, Inc. of Zhuhai (SZSE:000651)

- **Ticker / listing:** Shenzhen Stock Exchange, 000651
- **Where they compete:** Primarily China's #1 or #2 domestic residential-air-conditioner brand, but its product line also includes refrigerators, washing machines, kitchen appliances, and small appliances [`Haier Smart Home Co Ltd SHSE 600690 Competitors.rtf`, business description sourced from AB Electrolux (publ) 10-K filing, which names Gree as a home-appliance competitor alongside Haier]. Overlap with Haier's dominant refrigerator/kitchen-appliance segment exists but is secondary to Gree's core air-conditioner business — flagged as a partial segment fit, included because Gree is one of the three most commonly cited Chinese white-goods majors alongside Haier and Midea, and Haier's own filing places it directly against Gree in air conditioning ("公司中央空调国内市场份额同比提升 0.5 个百分点至 11.3%，位居行业前二" — Haier ranks #2 domestically in central air conditioning, implying Gree or another rival leads) [FY2025 Annual Report (SSE, CAS), Business Review, p.30].
- **Scale:** LTM total revenue $25,491.4m (LTM filing date 2026-04-28, USD, Capital IQ) vs. Haier's $44,028.5m on the same basis — Haier is ~1.73x Gree's revenue [`Company Comparable Analysis Haier Smart Home Co Ltd .xls`, tab: Financial Data].
- **Profitability / return on capital:** LTM gross margin 29.8%, LTM EBITDA margin 20.2%, LTM EBIT margin 17.4%, LTM net income margin 17.0% — roughly 2.5x Haier's LTM EBIT margin (6.9%) and 2.7x Haier's net margin (6.3%) on the identical comp-set basis [`Company Comparable Analysis Haier Smart Home Co Ltd .xls`, tab: Operating Statistics]. ROIC/ROE not disclosed in this comp export.
- **Source named in:** Capital IQ competitor export (third-party source document: AB Electrolux 10-K); independently corroborated by inclusion in Haier's own Capital IQ comparable-company set.
- **One-line read:** Smaller in overall revenue but far more profitable on every disclosed margin line — a materially higher-return operator concentrated in a single, higher-margin product category (air conditioning) rather than Haier's broader, thinner-margin multi-category mix.

### Competitor C — Whirlpool Corporation (NYSE:WHR)

- **Ticker / listing:** New York Stock Exchange, WHR
- **Where they compete:** North America and Latin America primarily — refrigerators, freezers, laundry appliances, cooking/kitchen appliances, and dishwashers under the Whirlpool, Maytag, KitchenAid, and other brands; directly overlaps with Haier's dominant refrigerator/kitchen-appliance segment, especially in North America where Haier competes through its GE Appliances brand (acquired 2016) [`Haier Smart Home Co Ltd SHSE 600690 Competitors.rtf`, business description sourced from AB Electrolux (publ) 10-K filing, which names Whirlpool as a home-appliance competitor alongside Haier; `02_business-identity.md` confirms GE Appliances as Haier's North America brand].
- **Scale:** FY2025 GAAP net sales $15,524m [Whirlpool Corporation, Fourth-Quarter and Full-Year 2025 Results press release, 2026-01-28 — Web, company's own results announcement, not in HAIER data pool]. Against Haier's FY2025 audited revenue of RMB302,329m (≈$42bn) or the $44,028.5m LTM figure in Haier's own Capital IQ comp set, Haier is roughly 2.8x Whirlpool's scale — at the outer edge of, but within, the ~5x comparable-scale threshold.
- **Profitability / return on capital:** FY2025 GAAP operating income $838m on $15,524m net sales = GAAP operating margin 5.4%; ongoing (non-GAAP) EBIT margin 4.7%; GAAP net earnings margin 2.2% [Whirlpool Corporation, Fourth-Quarter and Full-Year 2025 Results press release, 2026-01-28 — Web, unverified, not in HAIER data pool]. This is below Haier's own LTM EBIT margin of 6.9% and net margin of 6.3% [`Company Comparable Analysis Haier Smart Home Co Ltd .xls`, tab: Operating Statistics]. ROIC not stated in the source located; Whirlpool discloses a non-GAAP ROIC metric in its own filings but the specific FY2025 figure was not found in the sources checked — treat as not confirmed.
- **Source named in:** Capital IQ competitor export (third-party source document: AB Electrolux 10-K); Whirlpool is the most commonly cited global legacy peer to Haier in trade press given the two companies' direct North America rivalry (Whirlpool vs. GE Appliances).
- **One-line read:** The most scale-comparable non-Chinese peer, but running thinner operating and net margins than Haier on the most recent full year — a name-brand incumbent still absorbing US tariff and cost pressure that Haier's North America segment also flagged as a headwind.

## 3. Competitive Position

**Position: Gaining share** in the dominant segment. Haier states its China offline refrigerator retail-value share rose to 47.7% in FY2025, up 3.6 percentage points year on year, and that Haier's refrigerator and freezer retail volumes have ranked #1 globally for 18 and 15 consecutive years respectively (Euromonitor-sourced company claim) [FY2025 Annual Report (SSE, CAS), Business Review, "（四）产业经营分析 1、智慧大厨房 (1) 制冷产业", p.27]. The adjacent laundry-care segment shows the same pattern — domestic offline share up 1.9 points to 47.4%, and global washing-machine share rising to 14.4% (#1 globally, per Euromonitor as cited by the company) [FY2025 Annual Report (SSE, CAS), Business Review, p.29]. No independent (non-company) share-tracking source in the pool corroborates these Euromonitor-attributed figures, so this read rests on the company's own citation of a third-party data provider, not on the provider's report directly — a Level-3/4 claim, not Level-5. Partially offsetting: the FY2025 shareholder letter separately states that US tariffs and high interest rates hurt the North America segment's operating results, a profitability headwind that coexists with the share-gain claim rather than contradicting it [Preliminary Annual Report (HKEX Results Announcement), Mar-26-2026, "致股東的函件"].

## 4. Competitive Shape

The market is best read as fragmented globally but concentrated domestically. Globally, dozens of national and regional manufacturers compete in large appliances — the Capital IQ competitor export for Haier lists more than 50 distinct rival relationships spanning Whirlpool, Electrolux, Midea, Gree, LG Electronics, Samsung Electronics, BSH Hausgeräte (Bosch/Siemens, privately held), Panasonic, Arçelik, Hisense, Sharp, Daikin, and many India/Bangladesh-focused regional players [`Haier Smart Home Co Ltd SHSE 600690 Competitors.rtf`] — consistent with a fragmented global structure with no single dominant player (Haier's own claimed global refrigerator volume-share rank is #1, but no absolute global share percentage is disclosed in the pool). Within China specifically, the structure is concentrated among a small number of brands: Haier holds 47.7% offline refrigerator share, 47.4% washing-machine share, and 32.5% water-heater share domestically [FY2025 Annual Report (SSE, CAS), Chairman's Letter, p.3], with Midea and Gree as the next-largest named domestic rivals — consistent with an oligopoly-leaning domestic market led by these three groups, though the pool does not disclose Midea's or Gree's category-specific China refrigerator share needed to state a precise top-3 concentration ratio.

## 5. Caveat

Haier's own annual report (Chinese-language, SSE/CAS filing) discusses competitive rank in relative terms ("行业第二", "位居行业前二") without naming the specific rival company in the text reviewed, so none of the three profiled competitors above is "named by company" in the strict sense — all three are sourced from the Capital IQ third-party competitor-relationship export, cross-checked against Haier's own Capital IQ comparable-company set for two of the three (Midea, Gree). This is a real gap: a targeted search of Haier's own risk factors, MD&A, and available earnings-call transcripts in the pool (2019 vintage only — no recent transcript was in the pool) did not surface company-named competitors by name. BSH Hausgeräte (Bosch/Siemens) is a comparably large global rival named in the same Capital IQ export (LTM revenue $13.1bn as of a stale Dec-2014 figure) but is privately held as a subsidiary of Robert Bosch GmbH, so no current audited margin or return figure could be sourced for it — it was excluded from the three profiles for this reason, not because it is not credible. AB Electrolux (publ) (OM:ELUX B) is another highly credible, comparably scaled competitor (LTM revenue $13,463.41m per the Capital IQ export) that was considered but not profiled in the top 3 to keep the list to the most segment-relevant and best-evidenced peers; its FY2025 operating margin (2.8%, on SEK 131,282m net sales and SEK 3,657m operating income excluding non-recurring items) is available from its own year-end report [AB Electrolux/Electrolux Group, Year-end Report Q4 2025, 2026-01-30 — Web, unverified, not in HAIER data pool] and downstream `moat` may want it as a fourth peer data point.

## business-model / 09_moat.md

_Source: `business-model/09_moat.md`_

# Moat — HAIER

Upstream `08_competitive-map.md` is present (required). `07_business-quality.md` and `10_external-dependency.md` are present (optional, used for the through-cycle and cyclicality reads). No upstream gap to flag.

## 1. Named Competitors

(Inherited from `08_competitive-map.md` — all three sourced from the Capital IQ third-party competitor-relationship export, not named directly by Haier's own filing text.)

- **Competitor A — Midea Group Co., Ltd. (SZSE:000333).** Larger, more diversified Chinese appliance conglomerate (adds robotics/building tech/industrial segments); LTM revenue $68,169.1m, ~1.55x Haier's scale.
- **Competitor B — Gree Electric Appliances, Inc. of Zhuhai (SZSE:000651).** Smaller in revenue ($25,491.4m LTM, ~0.58x Haier) but concentrated in the higher-margin air-conditioning category; the most profitable of the three on every disclosed margin line.
- **Competitor C — Whirlpool Corporation (NYSE:WHR).** The most scale-comparable non-Chinese peer ($15,524m FY2025 net sales, ~0.35x Haier); Haier competes against it directly in North America through the GE Appliances brand.

## 2. Moat Sources

| Possible Moat | Present? (Y/N) | Evidence | Strength /100 |
|---|---|---|---:|
| Brand | Y (weak-mixed) | China offline share leadership: 47.7% refrigerator, 47.4% washing-machine, 32.5% water-heater [FY2025 Annual Report (SSE, China ASBE), Chairman's Letter, p.3-4]. Company claims global #1 refrigerator/freezer volume share for 18 consecutive years and #1 washing-machine share (Euromonitor-sourced company claim, not independently corroborated in the pool — Level 3/4, not Level 5) [same source, Business Review, p.27, p.29]. Premium Casarte sub-brand exists but is not broken out with its own margin line. This brand strength does NOT convert into a margin premium: Haier's LTM EBIT margin (6.9%) sits below both Midea (9.8%) and Gree (17.4%) on the identical Capital IQ comp-set basis [`Company Comparable Analysis Haier Smart Home Co Ltd .xls`, tab: Operating Statistics], and business-quality's own pricing-power row scores only 38/100, noting gross margin fell 460bp (30.9%→26.3%) over FY2021-FY2025 [`07_business-quality.md`, Pricing power row]. | 48 |
| Cost advantage | N / Not proven | Gross margin (26.3% LTM) is essentially tied with Midea (26.3%) and below Gree (29.8%) on the same comp-set basis [`Company Comparable Analysis Haier Smart Home Co Ltd .xls`, tab: Operating Statistics] — no evidence of a lower unit-cost structure than named peers. Raw materials are 84.0% of the appliance segment's cost of sales (up from 82.0% prior year), named as a top-ten principal risk, with no disclosed scale-driven procurement advantage over rivals [FY2025 Annual Report (China ASBE, SSE 600690), cost-structure table, p.23; `07_business-quality.md`, Commodity dependence row, 18/100]. | 15 |
| Distribution | Y (weak) | Owns the 日日順 (Rendanheyi/"Day&Day") logistics and channel network, brought fully into consolidation via a voting-rights entrustment in Dec-2024 [`11_capital-allocation-governance.md`, Restatements row]. Manufacturing and sales footprint spans 30+ countries. But this does not lock in the channel: distributors, retailers and online platforms "may place orders with us at such time and in such quantities as they deem appropriate" — no long-term contract or minimum-volume commitment exists with any channel partner [FY2025 Annual Report (HKEX, IFRS), "Relationship with Customers", p.80, cited in `05_customer-geography.md` §1 and `07_business-quality.md` Customer stickiness row]. Reach is real; contractual protection of that reach is not. | 38 |
| Scale | Y (weak-mixed) | Haier claims global #1 volume share in refrigerators (18 years) and washing machines, and is ~1.73x Gree's revenue and ~2.8x Whirlpool's [`08_competitive-map.md` §2]. But Midea is ~1.55x Haier's own revenue, so Haier is not the largest player in its own peer set, and — critically — its greater scale in refrigeration/appliances than Gree and Whirlpool has not produced a margin advantage: Haier's EBIT margin (6.9%) is below both Midea's (9.8%) and Gree's (17.4%) [same comp-set source as above]. Scale exists; it is not converting into superior unit economics. | 42 |
| Technology / IP | N / Not proven | R&D expense was RMB10,095.9m in FY2025, 3.3% of RMB302,346.8m total revenue [`Haier Smart Home Co Ltd SHSE 600690 Financials (2).xls`, Income Statement tab, R&D Exp. and Total Revenue, FY2025 column]. No patent count, IP litigation win, or technology licensing revenue is disclosed anywhere in the pool. Business-quality's own read: "smart home" features are incremental, not category-redefining, in the filings' own MD&A language, and the industry rate-of-change score (72/100) reflects a mature, slow-changing technology base shared by all named peers [`07_business-quality.md`, Industry rate-of-change row]. | 25 |
| Licenses / regulation | N / Not proven | No exclusive license, quota, or regulatory protection specific to Haier is disclosed. EU F-Gas and energy-efficiency rules are cited as a demand tailwind for the commercial-refrigeration line, but this benefits any compliant manufacturer in the category, not Haier uniquely [`10_external-dependency.md`, Regulation row]. Regulation in this filing set reads as a dependency (tariffs, subsidy cliffs) rather than a protective moat. | 12 |
| Network effects | N | Home appliances are single-unit durable-good purchases with no multi-sided platform or usage-based network dynamic disclosed anywhere in the pool. | 5 |
| Switching costs | N | Business-quality found no contractual lock-in anywhere in the distribution chain, and "end-consumer repurchase is a fresh competitive decision each cycle, not an automatic renewal" [`07_business-quality.md`, Customer stickiness row, scored 32/100]. Top-5 customers are only 19.6% of FY2025 sales with no severe-dependence certification needed [FY2025 Annual Report (SSE, China ASBE), Section 3(7)A/B, pp.43-44]. | 10 |
| Natural resource access | N | Haier does not own or control upstream commodity supply (steel, aluminium, copper, plastics/foam) — these are purchased inputs, hedged via forwards/futures under an internal policy, not a proprietary resource position [`10_external-dependency.md`, Commodity prices row, §3]. Commodity dependence is a disclosed risk, not an advantage. | 5 |
| Location advantage | N / Not proven | The company has actively relocated European production toward Turkey/Southeast Asia/China re-export routes to blunt US/EU tariff exposure [`10_external-dependency.md` §3]. This is a real, evidenced operational capability (adaptive manufacturing footprint) but it is a management response to trade policy, not a structural cost or access advantage tied to a specific, hard-to-replicate location (e.g., proximity to a unique input or port). Not counted as a moat source. | 15 |

No single source clears the "strong" band (61+). The two least-weak sources — Brand (48) and Scale (42) — are both real and evidenced but neither converts into superior margins versus the two named Chinese peers (Midea, Gree); Distribution (38) is undermined by the absence of any channel lock-in. This is a company with structural presence in several of the ten categories, but no source strong enough on its own to explain a durable profit gap in the company's favor — the opposite gap (Haier trailing two of three named peers on margin) is the more visible pattern.

## 3. Competitive Economics

| Company / Competitor | Gross Margin | EBIT Margin | Return on capital (ROIC) | Period | Source |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| Haier Smart Home (600690) | 26.3% | 6.9% | 7.97% (FY2025); 8.32% (FY2021–FY2025 avg); 7.56% (LTM) | LTM as of comp-set date 2026-08-12 (margins); FY2021–FY2025 / LTM Mar-2026 (ROIC) | `Company Comparable Analysis Haier Smart Home Co Ltd .xls`, tab: Operating Statistics (margins); `Haier Smart Home Co Ltd SHSE 600690 Financials (2).xls`, tab: Ratios, Return on Capital % row (ROIC) |
| Competitor A — Midea Group (000333) | 26.3% | 9.8% | Not disclosed | LTM filing date 2026-04-29 | `Company Comparable Analysis Haier Smart Home Co Ltd .xls`, tab: Operating Statistics, per `08_competitive-map.md` §2 |
| Competitor B — Gree Electric (000651) | 29.8% | 17.4% | Not disclosed | LTM filing date 2026-04-28 | `Company Comparable Analysis Haier Smart Home Co Ltd .xls`, tab: Operating Statistics, per `08_competitive-map.md` §2 |
| Competitor C — Whirlpool (WHR) | Not disclosed in pool (GAAP net sales $15,524m) | 5.4% (GAAP operating margin) | Not confirmed | FY2025 (year ended Dec-2025) | Whirlpool Corporation, Fourth-Quarter and Full-Year 2025 Results press release, 2026-01-28 — Web, unverified, not in HAIER data pool, per `08_competitive-map.md` §2 |

**The economic moat test.**

> Return on capital **above** cost of capital: **8.32% ROIC** (FY2021–FY2025 through-cycle average, Capital IQ "Return on Capital %") vs **≈3.9%–4.8% WACC** (CAPM estimate — *Inference, not from filings*) — a gap of roughly **350–440 basis points**.

- **Metric match.** Haier is a generic operating manufacturer (business-identity found no matching row in `frameworks/SECTOR_OVERLAYS.md` — not a bank, insurer, or REIT [`07_business-quality.md` §"Sector overlay"]), so ROIC vs WACC is the correct pair, not ROE vs cost of equity.
- **Return-on-capital source and cross-check.** The primary figure is Capital IQ's own "Return on Capital %" series: 7.88% (FY2021), 8.12% (FY2022), 8.51% (FY2023), 9.12% (FY2024, the cyclical peak), 7.97% (FY2025), 7.56% (LTM Mar-2026) [`Haier Smart Home Co Ltd SHSE 600690 Financials (2).xls`, tab: Ratios]. As a cross-check against the "standard base" (NOPAT ÷ average invested capital), a manual FY2025 build gives: EBIT RMB20,866.8m × (1 − 14.1% effective tax rate) = NOPAT RMB17,921.4m, divided by average Total Capital (Total Debt + Total Equity, including minority interest) of RMB163,548.1m (FY2024 RMB158,449.7m / FY2025 RMB168,646.5m average) [`Haier Smart Home Co Ltd SHSE 600690 Financials (2).xls`, tabs: Income Statement, Balance Sheet] = **10.96%** — materially *higher* (less conservative) than Capital IQ's reported 7.97% for the same year. The two cannot be fully reconciled from the pool exports (Capital IQ's exact averaging window and capital-base definition are not disclosed), so per CLAUDE.md §4's conservative-default rule, **this report uses the lower, vendor-computed 7.97% (FY2025) / 8.32% (5-yr average) figure**, not the higher manual estimate, for the verdict below. Haier does not disclose its own headline ROIC/ROCE metric anywhere in the pool (only a company-disclosed weighted-average ROE of 16.98% for FY2025, close to Capital IQ's own ROE of 16.47% [FY2025 Annual Report (SSE, China ASBE), 主要财务指标 table, p.12] — not the metric this test uses, but shown for completeness).
- **Tax-rate normalization.** The 14.1% FY2025 effective tax rate used above is structural, not a distorted single-year figure: the effective rate declined smoothly from 16.97% (FY2021) to 13.54% (LTM Mar-2026) with no visible one-off spike or dip, and no FVTPL fair-value loss, one-off deferred-tax charge, or settlement item was found in the pool for Haier [`Haier Smart Home Co Ltd SHSE 600690 Financials (2).xls`, tab: Ratios, Effective Tax Rate % row]. No `valuation/04_intrinsic-dcf` output exists yet in this pool to reconcile against — this rate is the anchor for that module when it runs.
- **Through-cycle basis.** FY2024's 9.12% print is the cyclical high-water mark, not the run rate — business-quality independently found the same pattern (ROIC "peaked at 9.1% in FY2024 and pulled back to 8.0% in FY2025 and 7.6% on an LTM basis," a subsidy-assisted high, not a structurally rising return) [`07_business-quality.md` §4]. The verdict below uses the 5-year (FY2021–FY2025) average of 8.32%, not the FY2024 peak.
- **Net-cash basis check.** Haier held net cash of −RMB16,975.1m (strict basis, total debt minus cash & short-term investments) at Dec-2025 [`11_capital-allocation-governance.md`, Debt level row] — about 10% of the RMB168,646.5m FY2025 Total Capital base. Capital IQ's own "Total Capital" figure already does **not** net out cash (it sums Total Debt + Common Equity + Minority Interest with no cash subtraction) [`Haier Smart Home Co Ltd SHSE 600690 Financials.xls`, tab: Key Stats, "Total Capital includes Common Equity and Total Liability"], so the reported ROIC is already a gross-capital figure — no further net-cash inflation adjustment is needed, and the modest net-cash position does not distort the through-cycle read.
- **Cost-of-capital source.** No company-disclosed WACC, cost-of-equity, or hurdle rate was found anywhere in the pool. Per the §3 source-priority (company-disclosed → CAPM estimate, labelled → not determinable), a CAPM estimate is used, **labelled Inference, not from filings**: risk-free rate 1.70% (China 10-year government bond yield, Aug-2026 [Web: tradingeconomics.com, 2026-08-07, unverified]); beta 0.46 (5-year, Capital IQ) [`Company Comparable Analysis Haier Smart Home Co Ltd .xls`, tab: Operating Statistics; corroborated by `Haier Smart Home Co Ltd SHSE 600690 Public Company Profile.rtf`, "Beta 5Y: 0.46"]; equity-risk-premium assumption 6.5% (mid-point inference for China, not sourced from a filing) → cost of equity ≈ 4.7%. Pre-tax cost of debt 1.699% is the current yield-to-worst on Haier's own Jun-2028 senior unsecured RMB note [`Haier Smart Home Co Ltd SHSE 600690 Fixed Income Securities Summary.rtf`] → after-tax cost of debt ≈ 1.46% (at the 14.1% normalized tax rate). Weighted at the market-based capital structure (Total Debt RMB42,076.8m / Total Capital RMB176,870.6m = 23.8% debt weight) [`Haier Smart Home Co Ltd SHSE 600690 Financials.xls`, tab: Key Stats] gives **WACC ≈ 3.9%**. Sensitivity to a more conservative 9% ERP assumption raises this to **≈4.8%** — the ROIC-above-WACC gap narrows from ~440bp to ~350bp but the sign does not flip under either assumption.

## 4. Where The Company Sits

1. **Relative to peers.** Company sits toward the **bottom** of named peers on margin: Haier's LTM EBIT margin (6.9%) and net margin (6.3%) rank 3rd of the four names in this set — below Gree (17.4% EBIT / 17.0% net) and Midea (9.8% EBIT / 9.6% net), ahead only of Whirlpool (5.4% GAAP operating margin / 2.2% GAAP net margin) [`08_competitive-map.md` §2; `Company Comparable Analysis Haier Smart Home Co Ltd .xls`, tab: Operating Statistics]. On gross margin Haier (26.3%) roughly ties Midea (26.3%) and trails Gree (29.8%).
2. **Absolute (the economic moat test).** The company earns a return on capital **above** its estimated cost of capital: **8.32% ROIC** (5-yr through-cycle average) vs **≈3.9%–4.8% WACC** (CAPM inference) — a gap of roughly 350–440 basis points that survives the ERP sensitivity check.

## 5. Moat Verdict

**Narrow moat.**

The company clears the absolute economic test — through-cycle ROIC (8.32%) sits above even a conservatively-sensitized cost-of-capital estimate (≈3.9%–4.8%) — so this is not the "moat in structure, not economics" failure case. But it cannot be called Strong: none of the ten possible sources scored above 48/100, the two least-weak (Brand 48, Scale 42) are both real but do not convert into peer-superior economics, and Haier's own profitability sits at the bottom of its three named peers rather than the top — a company earning below two of three named rivals on every disclosed margin line is not exercising pricing power over them, even if it beats its own cost of capital in absolute terms. The clearest evidence a moat exists at all is that ROIC has stayed above a very low China-linked WACC through a full five-year window without dropping to breakeven; the clearest evidence it is not strong is that Gree, with a fraction of Haier's scale, earns roughly 2.5x Haier's EBIT margin in the same country and adjacent product categories.

**Moat trajectory: eroding.** Gross margin fell 460bp over five years (30.9% FY2021 → 26.3% FY2025), a real multi-year step-down the company itself attributes partly to Q4 copper/commodity price rises overwhelming its cost-reduction program [`07_business-quality.md`, Pricing power row]. ROIC has now declined for two consecutive readings from its FY2024 peak — 9.12% (FY2024) → 7.97% (FY2025) → 7.56% (LTM Mar-2026) [`Haier Smart Home Co Ltd SHSE 600690 Financials (2).xls`, tab: Ratios]. This is happening even as Haier gains nominal China market share (offline refrigerator share +3.6pp to 47.7% in FY2025 [`08_competitive-map.md` §3]) — the combination (share up, margin and return on capital down) is consistent with share being defended or gained through price/promotion rather than through pricing power, the opposite of a widening moat. Business-quality's competitive-intensity row (24/100, "one of the most crowded consumer-durables categories globally") and the segment map's own flagged "price-war risk in a fragmented, oversupplied sub-industry" for Air Solutions corroborate the same direction [`07_business-quality.md`, Competitive intensity row]. Because business-quality's industry rate-of-change score (72/100) rules out a fast-changing-industry discount, this erosion reads as competitive/cost-pass-through pressure in a stable-technology category, not disruption — a slower-moving but still real threat to durability. Over the next five years the test this narrow moat would need to pass is whether gross margin and ROIC stabilize once the China trade-in subsidy fully laps and commodity costs normalize, or whether the gap to Gree and Midea keeps widening.

## business-model / 10_external-dependency.md

_Source: `business-model/10_external-dependency.md`_

# External Dependency Check — HAIER

Note on scope: Haier Smart Home Co., Ltd. (SSE: 600690 / HKEX: 6690) is a Chinese-incorporated, globally-manufacturing home-appliance group (refrigerators, washers, air conditioners, kitchen and water appliances, plus commercial refrigeration/HVAC via the acquired Carrier Commercial Refrigeration — "CCR" — business and GE Appliances in North America). Figures below are read from the FY2025 A-share annual report (China ASBE standard, filed to the Shanghai Stock Exchange) and the FY2025 H-share annual report (IFRS, filed to HKEX) — same fiscal year (ended 2025-12-31), reconciled rather than averaged per CLAUDE.md §15/§27.

## 1. Dependency Table

| External Variable | Dependency Level (Low / Mid / High) | Why It Matters | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Commodity prices | **High** | Raw materials (steel, aluminium, copper, plastics, foam) are 84.0% of the household-appliance segment's cost of sales in FY2025 (up from 82.0% in FY2024) — the single largest cost line by far. The company names this explicitly as one of its ten disclosed principal risks, and its own MD&A attributes FY2025's 1.1-percentage-point gross-margin decline (to 26.7%) partly to "continued Q4 rises in copper and other bulk materials" in the domestic market, which offset its cost-reduction program. | FY2025 Annual Report (China ASBE, SSE 600690), p.58, item 3 ("原材料价格波动的风险" — raw-material price volatility risk); cost-structure table, p.23 (原材料 15,554,203万元 / 84.0% of 主营业务成本, vs 82.0% prior year); MD&A margin discussion, p.22 ("国内市场四季度铜等大宗材料持续上涨...毛利率同比下降") |
| Interest rates | **Low-Mid** | 70% of FY2025 borrowings (RMB25,468m of RMB36,382m total) are floating-rate; a disclosed 1-percentage-point rate move changes after-tax profit by only RMB273m (2024: RMB253m) — under 1.5% of FY2025 net profit attributable to owners (RMB19,553m). The company holds net cash on a broad basis (cash & short-term investments RMB66,675m vs total debt RMB42,077m per CapIQ), which caps the real damage a rate move can do. | FY2025 Annual Report (HKEX, IFRS), Note 43 "利率風險", p.301 (floating-rate table and RMB273m sensitivity); Capital IQ Key Stats export (cash & ST investments RMB66,675.5m; total debt RMB42,076.8m) |
| FX | **Mid** | Overseas revenue is 51.4% of total (RMB154,545m of RMB300,582m main-business revenue), with sales/purchases and borrowings denominated in USD, EUR, JPY and other currencies, and the parent's consolidated statements are in RMB while subsidiaries report in local functional currencies. The company runs a hedging program (forwards, NDFs, options, cross-currency swaps) explicitly "to avoid and prevent FX risk," and the disclosed transactional sensitivity is small — a 5% RMB move vs USD/EUR/JPY moves FY2025 pre-tax profit by only RMB128m / RMB94m / RMB12m respectively (all under 1% of net profit). But that sensitivity table only covers monetary assets/liabilities at period-end, not full P&L/margin translation exposure — FY2025's finance-expense ratio improved 0.36pp specifically because "the Euro and other currencies appreciated, increasing FX gains," showing the P&L is not fully insulated. | FY2025 Annual Report (China ASBE, SSE 600690), p.42 (domestic revenue RMB146,036m / overseas RMB154,545m), p.58 item 6 ("汇率波动风险"), p.22 (finance-expense ratio improvement from Euro appreciation); FY2025 Annual Report (HKEX, IFRS), Note 43 "外幣風險", p.299-300 (5% sensitivity table) |
| Freight / logistics rates | **Low-Mid** | The shareholder letter cites the continuing Russia-Ukraine war and a Red Sea shipping crisis as sources of 2025 "market disruption costs" the company had to absorb, alongside tariffs — but no freight-cost figure or margin impact is separately quantified anywhere in the filing. | FY2025 Annual Report (China ASBE, SSE 600690), p.3 ("俄乌战争还在继续，红海再叠加危机"; "消化了各种市场扰乱成本") |
| Government policy | **High** | China's national appliance trade-in subsidy program ("国补" — 15% of final sale price, capped at RMB1,500/unit, on energy/water-efficient fridges, washers, ACs and three other categories) is a direct, named driver of Chinese demand. The company's own outlook flags that "under the pressure of a high base from the subsidy years, 2026 industry-wide growth is expected to face pressure," and separately attributes softer 2025 China retail conditions partly to "the fading effect of the appliance subsidy policy." | FY2025 Annual Report (China ASBE, SSE 600690), p.3 ("家电补贴政策效应的递减"); p.20-21 (2026 outlook — subsidy scope/rate detail and high-base growth-pressure warning, "国补较高基数压力下，2026年行业整体增长预计有所承压") |
| Regulation | **Mid** | Regulation cuts both ways here. EU energy-efficiency rules and F-Gas refrigerant regulation are cited as demand *tailwinds* forcing mandatory replacement of high-GWP commercial refrigeration equipment — a source of the CCR (commercial refrigeration) segment's growth. Conversely, US/EU tariff and trade rules are a demand and cost *headwind* (see Geopolitics row). No numeric compliance-cost figure is disclosed. | FY2025 Annual Report (China ASBE, SSE 600690), p.13-14 (EU F-Gas-driven "強制清場" replacement demand; EU energy-efficiency standard tightening) |
| Weather | **Low-Mid** | India's air-conditioner sales were hit by "an unfavorable season" in 2025 per the company's own market commentary — a direct, named weather-linked demand swing in one regional product line, but not quantified and not company-wide. | FY2025 Annual Report (China ASBE, SSE 600690), p.4 ("家电行业遇到影响空调产品销售的不利季节" — South Asia/India section) |
| Geopolitics | **High** | The single most repeated theme in the shareholder letter: large US tariffs on Chinese-made appliance exports forced supply-chain reconfiguration for high-end products shipped to the US; "regional protectionism and non-tariff barriers" are named as making overseas expansion structurally harder; the North America segment's results are explicitly said to have been "impacted by tariffs and other factors" in 2025, and overseas gross margin gains were "offset by high tariffs." Management's own 2026 outlook still treats this as unresolved ("supply-chain restructuring... tariff impact will gradually ease in 2026" — a forecast, not a fact). | FY2025 Annual Report (China ASBE, SSE 600690), p.3 ("美国对中国出口的家电产品施以大额关税...北美区受关税等因素影响了经营业绩"); p.58 item 5 ("关税增加的风险"); p.22 (overseas gross-margin offset by "关税高企"); p.5 (2026 outlook, tariff easing expectation) |
| Consumer cycle | **High** | Listed as the company's own #1 disclosed risk: a household appliance is a durable good, so demand tracks disposable income and income-growth expectations, and a slowing property market indirectly depresses appliance demand. The letter separately cites "high US interest rates plus tariff-driven inflation" curbing US appliance consumption, and a "weak Chinese property market" pressuring Chinese retail. | FY2025 Annual Report (China ASBE, SSE 600690), p.58, item 1 ("宏观经济增速放缓导致市场需求下降的风险"); p.3 ("美国高利率叠加关税通胀，影响了美国家电消费...中国房地产市场疲软...给中国家电零售市场带来了波动和价格下行冲击") |
| Industrial cycle | **Low-Mid** | The commercial refrigeration/HVAC piece (CCR, acquired from Carrier; plus "大暖通" commercial-building HVAC) carries some B2B/capex-cycle exposure — CCR delivered 16% growth in Asia-Pacific in its first full year post-close — but this is a minority of group revenue relative to the consumer-appliance core, and no capex-cycle sensitivity is separately quantified. | FY2025 Annual Report (China ASBE, SSE 600690), p.4 (CCR "远超行业的16%增长" in Asia-Pacific), p.13 (commercial refrigeration/HVAC market discussion) |

## 2. Sensitivity, If Disclosed

| Variable | Disclosed Move | Disclosed Impact (FY2025) | Disclosed Impact (FY2024, restated) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RMB vs USD | ±5% | ∓RMB128m pre-tax profit | ∓RMB159m | FY2025 Annual Report (HKEX, IFRS), Note 43, p.300 |
| RMB vs EUR | ±5% | ∓RMB94m pre-tax profit | ∓RMB249m | FY2025 Annual Report (HKEX, IFRS), Note 43, p.300 |
| RMB vs JPY | ±5% | ±RMB12m pre-tax profit (inverse-signed vs USD/EUR) | ±RMB4m | FY2025 Annual Report (HKEX, IFRS), Note 43, p.300 |
| Interest rate (floating-rate borrowings) | ±1 percentage point | ∓RMB273m after-tax profit | ∓RMB253m | FY2025 Annual Report (HKEX, IFRS), Note 43, p.301 |

None of the FX or rate sensitivities disclosed above exceed roughly 1.5% of FY2025 net profit attributable to owners (RMB19,553m — FY2025 Annual Report (China ASBE, SSE 600690), p.3). No commodity-price sensitivity table (e.g., "a 10% copper price move changes gross margin by X bps") is disclosed anywhere in either annual report — the 84%-of-COGS raw-material weight (Section 1 above) and the FY2025 margin-decline commentary are the only quantified windows into that exposure, and they are a cost breakdown and a narrative attribution, not a formal sensitivity table.

## 3. Classification

**Partly externally driven.** Haier controls real, demonstrated levers — brand and channel execution (China refrigerator/washer/water-heater share leadership at 47.7% / 47.4% / 32.5%, FY2025 Annual Report (China ASBE, SSE 600690), p.4; GE Appliances #1 in the US for four straight years and high-end revenue +7% despite tariffs, p.4), disciplined FX/rate/commodity hedging programs (forwards, NDFs, swaps, commodity futures hedging under a dedicated internal policy, p.35-37), and active supply-chain relocation (Europe production shifted toward Turkey/Southeast Asia/China re-export routes to blunt tariff exposure, p.16). But four variables it does not control — raw-material commodity prices, the Chinese national trade-in subsidy cliff, US/global tariff policy, and the broader consumer/property cycle in both China and the US — are each independently named by the company itself as principal risks, and at least two of them (commodities, tariffs) are shown in the FY2025 numbers actually moving the reported gross margin. This is not a business whose outcomes are a pure pass-through to any single external variable, but it is also not a business where external variables are background noise.

## 4. External Dependency Risk Score

**52/100** (inverted scale — higher = worse / more externally dependent).

This sits in the 41-60 "material external exposure, mixed mitigation" band. It is pushed toward the middle-upper part of that band because four separate variables (commodities, government subsidy policy, tariffs/geopolitics, consumer cycle) are simultaneously High, and two of them (commodities, tariffs) are shown by the company's own FY2025 numbers to have actually dented gross margin (-1.1pp) despite active mitigation — not merely a disclosed risk that never bites. It is kept out of the 61-80 band because the financially hedgeable variables (FX, interest rates) are demonstrably well-managed (disclosed sensitivities under 1.5% of net profit), and the company shows real, executed management levers — supply-chain relocation, share gains in both the US and China, brand-driven price/mix — that are moving results in the opposite direction from the external headwinds.

## 5. The Single Biggest Lever

Raw-material commodity prices (steel, aluminium, copper, plastics/foam) — at 84% of the appliance segment's cost of sales (FY2025 Annual Report (China ASBE, SSE 600690), p.23), a 20% adverse move in input costs, if only partially passed through, would do more group-wide margin damage than any single tariff or FX shock, because it hits both the domestic and overseas businesses simultaneously and is already shown (Q4 2025 copper) to overwhelm the company's own cost-reduction program.

## 2. Classification

**Standard professional management.** The balance sheet is run conservatively (net cash on a strict basis, Total Debt/EBITDA under 1.5x), the dividend is generous and covered, buybacks have started and the share count is drifting down, the auditor relationship is clean and unqualified with no recent change, and the controlling shareholder's shares carry no pledge. None of this reaches "owner-operator discipline," though, because a material and growing slice of the balance sheet's cash management runs through an affiliated party — up to RMB33,988m, or roughly 57% of the Group's cash & short-term investments, sits with the Haier Group's own finance company rather than an independent bank — and roughly 5% of revenue-equivalent volume flows through other related-party goods/services agreements every year. None of these signals individually reaches disqualifier scale (the ~5% goods/services related-party-transaction ratio sits well under the 25% disqualifier-scan threshold, and no promoter pledging, audit qualification, or going-concern flag was found), so this is a monitoring item, not a governance red flag.

## 3. Most Material Signal

The related-party transaction row is the one signal that would change this classification if it deteriorated. The Group already parks the majority of its cash with an affiliated, non-independent finance company and has sharply increased its borrowing from that same entity (RMB196m in 2024 to RMB3,767m in 2025, against a RMB10,000m cap) — a pattern that is fully disclosed, independent-director-reviewed, and auditor-confirmed under HKEX Rule 14A.56 today, but which concentrates counterparty and liquidity risk inside the controlling shareholder's own financial arm rather than diversified independent banks. If the cap utilization kept climbing, or if pricing terms stopped tracking independent-bank benchmarks as management currently states they do, this would move the classification from "standard professional management" to "governance red flags."

## 4. Capital Allocation Score /100

**66/100.**

This reflects genuinely disciplined signals — net cash balance sheet, low and stable leverage, a covered and growing dividend, a share count that is flat-to-down, no promoter pledging, and a clean three-year unqualified audit history on both the CAS and IFRS books — offset by the related-party financial-services dependency (the largest weight in this score), a working-capital trend that is drifting the wrong way (cash conversion cycle less negative, DSO up ~8 days over two years), and a large, debt-assisted 2016 acquisition (GE Appliances, $5.6bn) that — while apparently well-integrated given its CEO's subsequent elevation to the main board — was material relative to the company's size at the time.

**Rejector-filter cap:** not applied. The acquisition-pattern row scored 35/100, well under the 70-severity trigger for a clear serial-acquirer pattern — the observed cadence (roughly one material third-party deal every 3-4 years, confined to the core appliance industry, with no evidence of forced divestitures or distracted core-franchise focus) does not meet the Filter 4 bar, so the 50/100 cap does not apply here.

## business-model / 12_red-flags-sweep.md

_Source: `business-model/12_red-flags-sweep.md`_

# Red Flags Sweep — HAIER

Company: Haier Smart Home Co., Ltd. — dual-primary listed A-share (SSE 600690, China ASBE basis) and H-share (HKEX 6690, IFRS basis). Figures below are FY2025 (ended 2025-12-31) unless stated, read from `Haier_Smart_Home_Co_Ltd_-_Form_Annual_Report(Mar-26-2026).pdf` (A-share, China ASBE, audited, unqualified) and cross-checked against the HKEX/IFRS FY2025 annual report and the Q1 2026 unaudited interim report (`Form_Interim_Report(Apr-27-2026)`). All Chinese-language sources are read and translated in full per CLAUDE.md §27 — the language of the filing is not treated as a data gap.

All six upstream specialist reports (`01`, `03`, `05`, `07`, `10`, `11`) are present and were read before this sweep. No upstream output missing.

## 1. Already Covered Upstream

| Upstream Agent | Flag Already Surfaced |
|---|---|
| disqualifier-scan | No auditor qualification/going-concern issue; no promoter pledge; related-party transactions well under 25% threshold; no auditor change; FY2024 restatement is an immaterial (0.01–0.05%), non-error common-control combination; no active regulator enforcement found; no single-customer concentration; positive operating cash flow all 4 years. Zero near-misses. |
| segment-map | "Other Business" catch-all is 13.0% of revenue with no product-level split (above the 10% materiality floor); no segment-by-geography profit matrix disclosed; FY2021→FY2022 segment-definition structural break flagged for downstream comparability. |
| customer-geography | Mainland China at 48.5% of revenue is a naked (non-contracted) geography concentration — all channels (China and overseas) place orders "at such time and in such quantities as they deem appropriate," with no minimum-volume commitment disclosed anywhere. |
| business-quality | Weak pricing power (score 38, gross margin down 460bp FY21→FY25); high commodity dependence (score 18, raw materials 84% of appliance COGS); high competitive intensity (score 24); high cyclicality (score 34) tied to China property and US rate/tariff cycles; weak customer stickiness (score 32, no contractual lock-in anywhere in the channel). |
| external-dependency | High dependency flagged on commodity prices, China trade-in subsidy (fading), US/EU tariffs and geopolitics, and the consumer cycle — external dependency risk scored 52/100 (inverted, material exposure). |
| capital-allocation-governance | Related-party financial-services concentration — up to RMB33,988m (~57% of group cash & short-term investments) parked with the Haier Group's own finance company, and related-party borrowing from that entity up 19x YoY (RMB196m→RMB3,767m); GE Appliances $5.6bn debt-assisted 2016 acquisition already flagged as the largest deal in the acquisition-pattern row; working-capital drift (cash conversion cycle -15.7 days FY23 → -3.4 days FY25, DSO +8 days); FY2024 common-control restatement (same item disqualifier-scan covers). |

## 2. New Red Flags

| Red Flag | Why It Matters | Evidence | Severity /100 *(higher = worse)* |
|---|---|---|---:|
| Goodwill + indefinite-life intangibles are ~25% of parent equity, concentrated in one 2016 deal, tested on unusually long (5–15 year) discounted-cash-flow budget periods, and never impaired | Goodwill of RMB27,300.2m plus indefinite-life intangibles of RMB2,705m (combined RMB30,005.2m) sit against parent-company equity of RMB118,698.4m — 25.3% of book equity is intangible-driven judgment, not hard assets. GE Appliances alone carries RMB20,883.0m of goodwill (17.6% of equity) from the 2016 acquisition and has never been impaired in nearly a decade, even though the North America segment — GEA's home market — is the one segment the company itself says was "impacted by tariffs" in FY2025 (already flagged by `05_customer-geography.md` and `10_external-dependency.md` as a tariff-exposed geography, but neither connects that exposure to the goodwill sitting behind it). The auditor named goodwill impairment a Key Audit Matter specifically because management's recoverable-amount test depends on judgment calls — revenue growth (2.61%–9.83%), EBITDA margin (1.98%–14.50%), perpetual growth (1.7%–2.0%) and discount rates (10.67%–15.55%) — over budget periods stretching up to 15 years, well beyond the 5-year explicit-forecast horizon that is standard practice; a longer budget period gives management more room to project a recovery from a currently-pressured segment before the terminal-value math has to carry it. | `FY2025 Annual Report (SSE, CAS), Note 七.21 (商誉), pp.189-190` — goodwill by CGU: GEA RMB20,883,014,420.11, Candy RMB2,129,809,642.73, CCR RMB2,329,305,898.20, other RMB1,958,099,676.33, total RMB27,300,229,637.37; same filing, Key Audit Matters section, p.115 (关键审计事项：商誉及使用寿命不确定无形资产的减值准备 — budget periods "5 到 15 年期不等", perpetual growth "1.7%-2.0%", revenue CAGR "2.61%-9.83%", EBITDA margin "1.98%-14.50%", pre-tax discount rate "10.67%-15.55%"); balance sheet, p.118 (归属于母公司所有者权益合计 RMB118,698,401,416.58; 使用寿命不确定无形资产账面价值 27.05亿元) | 50 |
| Foreign-subsidiary defined-benefit pension and post-retirement medical obligations (RMB1,293.5m net liability) not covered by any upstream report | Two subsidiaries run defined-benefit plans exposed to actuarial risk (discount-rate, mortality, medical-cost-trend assumptions) that a China-based reader could easily miss: Haier U.S. Appliance Solutions, Inc. (GE Appliances) runs a defined-benefit *post-retirement medical* plan for qualifying employees, and Carrier Refrigeration Benelux B.V. runs a defined-benefit *pension* plan. The combined net liability fell slightly from RMB1,372.9m to RMB1,293.5m in FY2025, but a re-measurement loss of RMB191.8m flowed through other comprehensive income in the year — a real, if modest (6.6% of FY2025 net profit attributable to owners), balance-sheet and earnings-volatility exposure with no upstream module coverage. | `FY2025 Annual Report (SSE, CAS), Note 七.40 (职工薪酬), pp.189-191` — "①子公司 Haier U.S. Appliance Solutions, Inc.设定受益计划" (post-retirement medical, defined-benefit); "②子公司 Carrier Refrigeration Benelux B.V 设定受益计划" (pension, defined-benefit); combined 设定受益计划净负债 期末余额 RMB1,293,486,439.31 vs 期初余额 RMB1,372,873,072.99; 重新计量设定受益计划变动额 RMB191,778,591.61 (FY2025) vs -RMB1,011,523.04 (FY2024) | 25 |

No further material flags identified beyond the two rows above and upstream coverage.

## 3. Most Severe New Flag

The goodwill/intangible concentration is the more material of the two new flags. A quarter of Haier Smart Home's parent-company book equity (25.3%) is intangible-asset judgment rather than hard, verifiable value, with three-quarters of that goodwill (RMB20,883.0m of RMB27,300.2m, 76%) sitting behind a single decade-old acquisition — GE Appliances — in the one region (North America) the company itself says tariffs are currently hurting. This is not evidence of impropriety: the audit opinion is unqualified, the impairment test is disclosed as a Key Audit Matter with the underlying assumptions shown, and no impairment charge would necessarily be warranted today. But the combination of a large intangible base, a 5–15 year discounted-cash-flow runway (longer than the 5-year explicit-period norm), and a currently-pressured segment sitting directly behind the largest CGU is exactly the setup where a future write-down — if tariff or consumer-cycle pressure in North America persists — would land as a sudden, non-cash but headline-grabbing hit to reported equity and earnings. The synthesizer should treat this as a monitoring item for the North America / GE Appliances thesis specifically, not as a standalone disqualifier.

## 4. Cross-Cutting Patterns

Both new flags in Section 2 trace back to the same event: the 2016 GE Appliances acquisition, already named upstream (`11_capital-allocation-governance.md`) as the largest deal in Haier's acquisition history. That single transaction is now the source of (a) the largest CGU by far in a goodwill balance that is a quarter of parent equity, and (b) part of the pension/OPEB obligation newly identified here (Haier U.S. Appliance Solutions is the GE Appliances entity). Combined with the external-dependency and customer-geography reports' independent finding that North America (26.4% of revenue, GE Appliances-led) is the segment currently absorbing US tariff costs, the pattern is that one nine-year-old acquisition still concentrates several distinct, only-loosely-connected risk types — goodwill-impairment judgment, actuarial/pension exposure, and tariff-driven margin pressure — inside a single operating entity. No individual piece rises to disqualifier scale, but a synthesizer weighing North America execution risk should know all three sit on the same asset.
